failure_modes.description: The assumption that traffic patterns serve as sufficient information for neighbors is fundamentally flawed. Traffic flow patterns are ambiguous and contain noise that makes interpretation unreliable.
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic engineers have long recognized that flow patterns alone cannot distinguish between temporary congestion and persistent demand, leading to inappropriate signal adjustments.

failure_modes.description: Direct contradicts established traffic engineering knowledge that centralized control or coordinated systems significantly outperform isolated intersection control.
failure_modes.evidence: Numerous studies show that coordinated signal systems can reduce travel time by 15-30% compared to isolated control, which this approach would essentially be.

failure_modes.description: The mechanism fails to account for non-traffic environmental factors that influence traffic patterns but are not part of the stigmergy feedback loop.
failure_modes.evidence: Weather events, accidents, and construction create traffic patterns that don't result from signal timing, creating false environmental signals that would mislead the system.

failure_modes.description: The core concept is not novel - isolated intersection control systems have been extensively studied and shown to be inferior to coordinated approaches.
failure_modes.evidence: The TRANSYT and SCATS systems from the 1970s already demonstrated the superiority of coordinated signal control over isolated methods.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis directly contradicts its own falsifier condition - it explicitly predicts failure for non-adjacent intersections.
failure_modes.evidence: The hypothesis admits it will fail for non-adjacent intersections, making it fundamentally unsuitable for real-world networks where intersections must coordinate beyond immediate neighbors.

failure_modes.description: The approach is incompatible with the actual target of traffic signal systems - optimizing network-wide performance rather than local efficiency.
failure_modes.evidence: Real-world traffic systems prioritize network-wide flow, not local intersection efficiency. A stigmergy approach would optimize for local metrics, creating Braess paradox situations where local improvements create global degradation.
